title: The Creature and the Creator
text:
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, published in 1818, is often read as an early work of science fiction, yet its deeper concern is the moral responsibility of the creator toward what he creates. Victor Frankenstein pursues the secret of life with an intensity that blinds him to the consequences of his ambition. When the creature finally opens its eyes, Victor recoils in horror and abandons it, a failure that the novel treats as the origin of all subsequent suffering. The narrative is told through layers of letters and recollections, which leave the reader unsure how much to trust any single voice.

The creature, left alone in a hostile world, learns language and morality by observing a cottage family through a crack in the wall. Shelley thus invites the reader to wonder whether cruelty is innate or whether it is produced by rejection and loneliness. Victor, meanwhile, grows increasingly isolated, and his refusal to acknowledge his own responsibility turns his guilt into a private obsession. The contrast between the eloquent creature and the self-pitying creator suggests that humanity is defined less by its origin than by the way it treats others.

According to the second paragraph, how does the creature learn language and morality?
options: By reading books in a library
By observing a cottage family through a crack in the wall
By being taught directly by Victor
By listening to letters read aloud

questions.text: What does Victor's reaction to the creature most suggest about his character?
options: He is confident in his scientific skill.
He is unable to accept responsibility for his own actions.
He values the creature above all else.
He has forgotten the purpose of his experiment.

questions.text: What is the most likely effect of the novel's framing through letters and recollections?
options: It makes the reader certain of every event.
It removes all moral ambiguity from the story.
It encourages the reader to question how reliable each narrator is.
It shows that science always produces happiness.

paragraph_translations: Frankenstein, de Mary Shelley, publicado en 1818, se lee a menudo como una obra temprana de ciencia ficción, pero su preocupación más profunda es la responsabilidad moral del creador hacia lo que crea. Victor Frankenstein persigue el secreto de la vida con una intensidad que lo ciega ante las consecuencias de su ambición. Cuando la criatura finalmente abre los ojos, Victor retrocede horrorizado y la abandona, un fracaso que la novela trata como el origen de todo el sufrimiento posterior. La narración se cuenta a través de capas de cartas y recuerdos, lo que hace que el lector no esté seguro de cuánto confiar en cada voz.

La criatura, abandonada en un mundo hostil, aprende el lenguaje y la moral observando a una familia de campesinos a través de una grieta en la pared. Shelley invita así al lector a preguntarse si la crueldad es innata o si la produce el rechazo y la soledad. Mientras tanto, Victor se aísla cada vez más, y su negativa a reconocer su propia responsabilidad convierte su culpa en una obsesión privada. El contraste entre la elocuente criatura y el creador lleno de autocompasión sugiere que la humanidad se define menos por su origen que por la manera en que trata a los demás.
